analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors to pay wages above the local poverty line for a family of four.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee after being introduced with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar federal agencies from signing contracts unless the contractor, and any subcontractor, pays workers wages and benefits above the federal poverty line for a family of four in the local area. It exempts genuine apprenticeship and job-training programs and businesses with 50 or fewer employees. The bill was sent to a House committee and then a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on federal service and supply contracts who are currently paid less than the local poverty line for a family of four. Their wages, including benefits like health insurance, would have to rise above that line, and subcontracted workers would be covered too [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: No federal agency could enter a contract unless it required wages and benefits (including health insurance) to exceed the poverty line for a family of four in the area where the work is done [S2][S3].
The requirement reaches down to subcontractors, so workers at the bottom of federal contracting chains would be covered, not just the prime contractor's employees [S3].
It carves out bona fide job training and apprenticeship programs and businesses with 50 or fewer employees, sparing entry-level training positions and small firms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and subcontractors who pay below-poverty wages would bear higher labor costs, some of which could be passed to the government through contract prices. Small businesses with 50 or fewer employees are exempt [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The exemption for businesses with 50 or fewer employees would leave many federally funded jobs uncovered and could push work toward small subcontractors [S2][S3].
Contractors would face higher labor costs, which they could pass on to federal agencies through higher contract prices, making the requirement partly a taxpayer cost [S2].
Tying the wage floor to the poverty line means the standard is relatively low and varies by family composition definitions rather than local living costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, targeted raise for the lowest-paid workers on federal contracts, at a cost mainly to those contractors and indirectly to taxpayers. It would not raise the general minimum wage and leaves small firms out, so its reach is limited — but what it does is straightforward and targeted at genuine hardship.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee in January 1997 and never received a hearing, a floor vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the Livable Wage Act on January 7, 1997 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Government Reform and Oversight the same day [S5].
On January 16, 1997 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 105th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors who pay below-poverty wages are better off, since no wage floor was ever imposed; the low-wage workers the bill aimed to help gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to raise sub-poverty wages and benefits on federal contracts, cutting into labor-cost savings. The requirement died in committee, so their status quo remained intact.

industries.industry: Small businesses (50 or fewer employees) holding federal contracts
industries.note: They were explicitly exempt from the wage requirement, but a higher cost on larger competitors could shift federal work toward them.
